strengths: Strong and clearly motivated contribution: the paper addresses a genuine, well-identified gap—no prior Gaussian rendering method achieves both projective exactness and real-time efficiency for generic cameras—and provides a coherent solution with three complementary components (exact ray-Gaussian transmittance, PBF association, BEAP sampling).

Solid mathematical foundation: the closed-form derivation of the ray-Gaussian integral via canonical transformation is clean, the connection to the 'maximum response' heuristic is insightful, and the appendix contains full derivations of gradients, numerical stability analysis, and PBF solvers, supporting reproducibility.

Efficient association design: the Particle Bounding Frustum replaces BVH traversal with closed-form quadratic solutions computed directly from the true 3D covariance, achieving very tight bounds (~475 Gaussians/tile vs 1377-2203 for UT/EWA), which convincingly explains the 2.5-5x association speedup and near-3DGS runtime.

Comprehensive evaluation: four datasets (ScanNet++, ZipNeRF, Aria, MipNeRF360) covering pinhole and fisheye settings, cross-camera generalization experiments, comparisons against relevant recent baselines (EVER, 3DGRT, 3DGUT, FisheyeGS), per-scene results, and stage-wise runtime breakdowns.

Thoughtful ablations: the paper isolates each component (transmittance replacement at training/test time, BEAP on/off, PBF vs EWA/UT association with cross-model evaluation), and includes a direct experimental rebuttal of the 'just scale up Gaussians' argument (Sec. 4.1) with strong evidence.

Honest treatment of limitations: the appendix clearly delineates what 'exactness' means, acknowledges ordering/self-occlusion approximations and popping artifacts, and discusses relations to 2DGS/HTGS formalisms.

Demonstrated generalization: training on narrow-FoV data and rendering extreme FoVs (170-180 degrees) where baselines fail, plus clear qualitative evidence of artifact reduction (grid-line artifacts, numerical instability in GOF).
weaknesses: The 'exactness' claim requires careful qualification: the method still relies on the maximum-response assumption, depth-based ordering, and independent Gaussian integration (ignoring self-attenuation), so it is exact only w.r.t. projective geometry, not physically correct volumetric rendering; the paper does acknowledge this, but the abstract/title framing slightly oversells.

Some comparisons are asymmetric: on Aria, only FisheyeGS is compared; on ScanNet++, 2DGS/HTGS-style methods are discussed but not directly benchmarked; a few tables mix numbers measured on different GPUs (4090/6000 Ada/5090) with normalization assumptions.

The BEAP gain, while consistent, is modest on pinhole scenes (0.3-2.0 dB), and part of the wide-FoV improvement conflates exact transmittance, exact association, and BEAP supervision; the component-wise attribution is provided but could be cleaner.

The evaluation protocol (reprojecting to native fisheye image space, central/peripheral region weighting) is method-specific and could introduce protocol sensitivity; details are in the appendix but full standardization against community benchmarks would strengthen claims.
Code is promised upon publication but not yet released at review time, limiting immediate reproducibility of the CUDA implementation, which is a substantial part of the contribution.
The mirror transformation trick (Sec. D.2) with a fixed empirical parameter (xi=1) is somewhat heuristic despite the otherwise principled derivations.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple datasets (ScanNet++, ZipNeRF, Aria, MipNeRF360) with both fisheye and pinhole settings, including a cross-camera generalization protocol that is genuinely interesting

The Particle Bounding Frustum (PBF) association is a well-engineered contribution: tight frustum-level association yields measurably fewer Gaussian duplications per tile (Tab. K.6) and translates into concrete 2.5-5x speedups in the association stage and ~5x overall speedup over exact ray-based baselines

Good ablation discipline: the paper isolates the effect of the transmittance formulation (Tab. 5, Sec. 4.4), the association scheme (Tab. K.6), and the BEAP supervision (Tab. 6), and the scaling study (Fig. 5, Tab. K.3) directly tests the Celarek et al. claim

Appendix material is thorough: full gradient derivations, numerical stability analysis with a demonstrated fix for GOF-style instability, and honest discussion of limitations (self-occlusion, ordering, popping artifacts)
Runtime analysis is done carefully with stage-wise breakdowns (Tabs. K.4, K.5) and cross-hardware FPS notes
weaknesses: Limited mathematical novelty at the core: the central 'closed-form transmittance' (Eq. 4 / Theorem 1) is the classical result that the line integral of an isotropic Gaussian is proportional to exp(-D^2/2), and the paper itself concedes this expression is equivalent to the 'maximum response' heuristic of Keselman & Hebert (2022) already used in 3DGRT/3DGUT. The claimed derivation 'from first principles' largely re-derives and re-interprets a known result rather than enabling new capability

'Projective exactness' is a self-defined notion (Appendix A) that excludes self-occlusion, ordering, and self-attenuation. Marketing the method as 'geometrically exact' while retaining depth-based sorting and the same max-response approximation as prior work overstates the contribution; the terminology invites confusion with truly exact volumetric rendering (e.g., EVER)

The BEAP representation is a relatively simple uniform angular sampling scheme; the claimed quality gains (Tab. 6) are modest (~0.3-0.4 dB) and could partly reflect sampling/resolution artifacts rather than a fundamentally better image-space parameterization

Fairness concerns in comparisons: 3DGEER uses BEAP supervision with GT color interpolation while several baselines use different training configurations and resolutions (1/8 FE vs 1/4 PH on ZipNeRF); FPS numbers mix measurements on RTX 6000 Ada / 5090 / 4090 with only footnotes, making speed comparisons imperfect

On the standard pinhole benchmark (MipNeRF360) the quality gains over 3DGUT/3DGS are marginal (e.g., +0.5 dB PSNR over 3DGUT), so the practical benefit is largely confined to wide-FoV/distorted settings; the broader significance for the general radiance-field community is narrower than the abstract suggests

Some central claims rest on qualitative evidence (grid-line artifacts in Fig. 1, popping artifacts relegated to supplementary videos), and the discussion of whether the max-response assumption error is 'negligible' leans on an external paper (Celarek et al.) rather than the authors' own analysis

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: 3DGEER derives a closed-form, projectively exact ray-Gaussian integral from first principles (Theorem 1), connecting and formalizing the previously heuristic 'maximum response' assumption, and provides a complete differentiable pipeline with full backward derivations and numerical stability analysis (Appendix B/C).

The Particle Bounding Frustum (PBF) association is a clever and practical contribution: exact frustum-level ray-particle association via quadratic tangency equations, avoiding BVH traversal overhead. The runtime analysis (Tab. K.4-K.6) is convincing, showing ~475 Gaussians/tile vs. 1377-2203 for EWA/UT and translating to real speedups.
BEAP is a simple but effective image-space representation that unifies FoV handling, aligns with the CSF partitioning, and shows consistent gains in ablations (Tab. 6, K.8).

Comprehensive evaluation across pinhole and fisheye benchmarks (MipNeRF360, ScanNet++, ZipNeRF, Aria) with strong baselines including recent concurrent work (3DGUT, EVER, HTGS). The cross-camera generalization setup and the scaling-vs-exactness study (Fig. 5, Sec. 4.1) directly address the strongest competing argument (Celarek et al., 2025).

Honest scoping of claims in Appendix A: the paper clarifies that 'exactness' refers to projective geometry only, and discusses ordering/self-attenuation limitations; numerical stability analysis in Sec. C.7/D.1 with the GOF comparison adds credibility.
Good reproducibility posture: detailed algorithms, implementation details, per-scene results, and a commitment to release code; supplementary code/video provided.
weaknesses: The exactness claim requires careful qualification: the method still relies on the maximum-response assumption and depth sorting, so it is not volumetrically exact in the same sense as EVER; the framing as 'geometrically exact' could be seen as somewhat oversold in the abstract, though the appendix is upfront about this.

Some per-scene results are mixed (e.g., Tab. K.2 where 3DGUT wins Storage/Kitchen, and EVER wins on some ZipNeRF splits in Tab. K.9), meaning the 'outperforms across all metrics' headline claim is slightly stronger than the per-scene evidence.

Novelty positioning relative to 2DGS/HTGS needed clarification (Sec. D.3 does address this, but the core closed-form integral is essentially the known maximum-response result); the strongest novelty lies in the angular-domain association (PBF) and BEAP, which are more engineering-oriented though well-validated.

ZipNeRF experiments use reduced resolutions (1/8 fisheye, 1/4 pinhole) which limits comparability to original benchmark numbers, and FPS comparisons in Tab. 4 mix measurements across different GPUs (footnoted, but still imperfect).

Generality to truly arbitrary camera models is asserted but experiments cover only pinhole, KB-fisheye, and Aria; e.g., full omnidirectional models or decentered/distorted industrial lenses are not demonstrated.
LLM-assisted writing is disclosed but some text quality issues remain (typos, e.g., 'demostrates', 'sucessfully'), which slightly detract from polish.
